rejected.question: In which year did Otis file its patent for a push-button control system that let riders call an elevator from each landing?

rejected.question: If an elevator car ever moved too fast, its safety jaws grip the guide rails and bring it to a stop within about how many inches?
rejected.fact: A speed-watching device called the governor trips at a preset speed limit and grips its own rope; that pulls a lever so the safety jaws under the car clamp the two main guide rails, bringing the cab to a halt in about 6.5 inches, according to TK Elevator.

sources.title: Governor Module - TK Elevator Classroom On Demand
sources.quote: Once the safety jaws engage the rails the cab will be brought to a halt in about 6.5 inches.

sources.title: Emergency Brake - TK Elevator Classroom On Demand
sources.quote: If an elevator cab begins to speed up or down the hoistway too quickly, the brake engages and securely brings the cab to a halt.

checks.reason: No independent source confirms a stopping distance of about 6.5 inches; the figure appears only on TK Elevator's own training page. Code-mandated stopping distances depend on speed: California's Table 3035 C (mirroring ASME A17.1 Table 2.17.3) gives 1 inch to 1 ft 3 in for elevators rated up to 125 fpm, 4 in to 1 ft 10 in at 200 fpm, and 14 ft to 40 ft 10 in at 1,500 fpm. That makes the distractors '60 inches' and '300 inches' legitimate stopping distances for faster elevators, so the question has no single correct answer as written. The governor-rope-lever-jaws mechanism itself is independently confirmed (LegalClarity, Firgelli), but the headline number is not.

checks.reason: The '6.5 inches' figure is TK Elevator's illustrative number for one slow installation, not a general fact. Stopping distance for Type B safeties is set by code as a function of governor-tripping speed (S = V²/81,144 + 0.84 ft max; S' = V²/231,840 ft min). California Elevator Safety Orders Table 3035 C: a 125 fpm car must stop within 1 in to 1 ft 3 in; a 500 fpm car within 1 ft 8 in to 5 ft 8 in; a 600 fpm car up to 7 ft 7 in. So the distractor 'About 60 inches' is a correct answer for an ordinary 500 fpm office elevator, and 'About 300 inches' is within code for a fast high-rise car. The premise (car 'moving too fast', emergency jaws clamping) is also accident-adjacent and potentially frightening for an anxious 7-12 year old. No small edit rescues both problems; a rewrite around the governor's name would be a different item.

items.question: Under California's elevator rules, how many steel hoisting ropes must a NEW traction elevator have at least?
items.fact: California's elevator safety rules (Title 8, section 3042) say a NEW traction elevator must have at least three hoisting ropes; ones already running on two may keep them. Together the ropes must be at least 7.6 times stronger than the loaded car needs. They are twisted steel cables linking the car to the counterweight over the drive sheave.

Section 1604.25 sits in Subchapter 4 (Construction Safety Orders), Article 14, Construction Hoists, and its Table 5 (7.60 at 50 fpm to 10.70 at 600 fpm) applies to construction hoists, not building elevators. California's Elevator Safety Orders, Section 3042, carry the same three-rope minimum for traction elevators (two for drum-type, with existing two-rope traction elevators grandfathered), and their Table 3042E1 runs from 7.60 at 50 fpm to 11.90 at 1,500 fpm for passenger elevators (6.65 to 10.55 for freight). items.question: What does an elevator's regenerative drive do with the electricity made when the car slows down?

items.fact: State laws such as Massachusetts' and Maine's say the inspector's certificate must be posted in (or right beside) the elevator car where riders can see it. Maine's law says every elevator must be inspected once a year.

items.question: A 'space elevator' would be a cable running from the ground up to a station in geostationary orbit, the orbit where a satellite stays above the same spot on Earth. About how high up is that orbit?
items.fact: Geostationary orbit is about 35,786 km up. A NASA report in 2000 said an Earth-to-orbit space elevator 'is not feasible today' because no material we can make yet is strong and light enough for such a long cable; carbon nanotubes, measured in the lab at about 100 times the strength of steel, are the hoped-for material.

The Earth to GEO space elevator is not feasible today ... carbon nanotubes that has exhibited laboratory strengths 100 times stronger than steel

The NASA study claims were checked against the full text of the companion NASA report CP-2000-210429 (Smitherman, Marshall SFC, August 2000, hosted by the International Space Elevator Consortium, not NTRS): it states GEO is 35,786 km in altitude, that 'The Earth to GEO space elevator is not feasible today', and that carbon nanotube materials 'exhibit strengths 100 times stronger than steel'. items.question: In Britain, which level of a building is called the 'first floor'?
items.answer: The level one above the street
items.fact: In British English the first floor is one level above the street (street level is called the ground floor), but in American English the first floor IS street level - so pressing '1' can take you to different places in London and New York.

Answer and fact accurate; distractor 'street level' is the genuine US sense, which is what makes the question work.

checks.quote: The first floor of a building is the floor immediately above the one at ground level. [British] regional note: in AM, use second floor 2. The first floor of a building is the one at ground level. [US] regional note: in BRIT, use ground floor

items.question: Muzak, the company whose name became a nickname for 'elevator music', got that name by mixing 'music' with the name of which company?
items.fact: The name Muzak dates from 1934. The company grew out of a 'wired radio' music service based on inventions by US Army general George Owen Squier, and the new name blends 'music' with the ending of the camera brand 'Kodak'. The name became so well known that people now call any gentle background music 'Muzak' or 'elevator music'.

sources.title: Encyclopedia.com: Muzak (St. James Encyclopedia of Popular Culture)
sources.quote: Squier's efforts to come up with a catchier name for his company, resulted in the term Muzak, a blend of the word 'music' with the final syllable from George Eastman's universally pronounceable synthetic trade name, Kodak.

sources.title: HistoryNet: Meet the Tech Visionary Who Started the U.S. Air Force, Built Phone Networks, and Invented Muzak
sources.quote: Over time, Muzak switched from the home consumer market to providing background music for hotels, restaurants, stores, and, most famously, elevators.

checks.reason: Independently confirmed on history.com and EBSCO Research Starters: Brigadier General George Owen Squier renamed his company Muzak in 1934, combining 'music' with 'Kodak'; history.com also ties the brand to 'elevator music'. One precision fix: the company itself predates 1934 (it was Wired Radio, Inc.); 1934 is when it took the Muzak name, so the fact now says that rather than 'began in 1934'.
checks.source_title: The Army General Who Invented Muzak | HISTORY
checks.quote: In 1934, Squier changed the company's name to Muzak — a combination of "music" and Kodak, one of the most successful companies of its day. (Second independent confirmation, EBSCO Research Starters: "Wired Radio, Inc., changed its name in 1934, when Squier decided to combine the word 'music' with 'Kodak,' the name of an already popular company, to get Muzak.")

checks.reason: The Kodak blend is confirmed by every source fetched (Encyclopedia.com and HistoryNet as cited; independently etymonline, History.com, Mood Media, Wikipedia citing Grove Music Online, Skeptoid). Two parts of the fact text are shaky, though: (1) 'Muzak began in 1934' — the firm (Wired Radio, Inc.) dates from 1922 and was RENAMED Muzak in 1934; Squier died March 1934, so 'started by' in 1934 is loose. (2) 'It later became famous for the background music played in elevators' is directly contradicted by Wikipedia (citing Skeptoid #370: 'this has never been one of their offerings'), while Mood Media (the successor firm) claims 1934 NYC elevator marketing — the point is contested, so the item should only claim the NICKNAME, which nobody disputes. Distractors (Ford, Coca-Cola, Disney) are unarguable. Content is child-safe. Reworded to keep the question on the nickname and the fact on the rename.

checks.quote: Though Muzak Holdings was for many years the best-known supplier of background music, and is commonly associated with elevator music, the company itself did not supply music to elevators.

items.question: In Europe, the lift accessibility rules say a narrow lift must have a mirror inside. What is the mirror for?
items.answer: So a wheelchair user can see behind them when backing out
distractors: To make the inside of the lift look bigger than it is
So that riders can check their hair before they arrive
To bounce light around the car and save electricity
items.fact: The European lift accessibility standard EN 81-70 requires a mirror in lift cars that are too narrow for a wheelchair to turn round. A passenger in a wheelchair has to reverse out, and the mirror lets them see what is behind them.

sources.title: iKONIC Lifts: Lift car requirements for EN 81-70:2021
sources.quote: Car types 1, 2 & 3 shall have a mirror to aid passengers in a wheel chair to see behind them.

sources.quote: Mirror is mandatory for car types 1, 2, and 3

The '300 mm above the floor' detail could NOT be fetched from any site independent of the researcher's two sources: LEIA's information note is download-only, BUT-SAN returns 403, and Elevator World is the researcher's own site (and behind a bot challenge). The fixed fact therefore drops the unverified 300 mm sentence and states the confirmed car-type rule instead.

checks.quote: Provide a mirror to enable a wheelchair user to observe obstacles behind them when moving backwards, if unable to turn around in the lift car. (KONE: "Mirror is mandatory for car types 1, 2, and 3")

Elevator World (cited) returned 403 so its quote is unverified. items.answer: The rope holding up his platform

items.fact: Otis's company history tells how at New York's Crystal Palace exhibition Elisha Otis stood on a platform lift high above the crowd and had the rope holding it cut with an axe. items.question: In which century did the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta write down rules for doing sums with zero?
items.fact: In the 7th century the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta wrote down rules for arithmetic with zero, such as 'the sum of zero and zero is zero'. Much earlier, by around 400 BC, Babylonian scribes were putting two little wedge marks in the place where we would write a 0 - a placeholder, not yet a number in its own right.

sources.title: MacTutor History of Mathematics: A history of Zero
sources.quote: Brahmagupta attempted to give the rules for arithmetic involving zero and negative numbers in the seventh century. … around 400 BC the Babylonians put two wedge symbols into the place where we would put zero to indicate which was meant.

checks.reason: Independent non-Wikipedia sources confirm the answer: storyofmathematics.com calls Brahmagupta 'the great 7th Century Indian mathematician' and says he 'established the basic mathematical rules for dealing with zero'; The Conversation (theconversation.com/nothing-matters-how-the-invention-of-zero-helped-create-modern-mathematics-84232) also calls him 'the seventh century Indian mathematician and astronomer Brahmagupta'. The Babylonian side-fact is corroborated by UT Dallas (personal.utdallas.edu/~gupta/dawn/zero.html: 'around 400 BC that the Babylonians put two wedge symbols') and a USU history page, but several other accounts date the two-slanted-wedge placeholder to about 300 BC, so the date is hedged in the fix. Answer and distractors are fine.
checks.source_title: The Story of Mathematics: Indian Mathematics - Brahmagupta
checks.quote: The great 7th Century Indian mathematician and astronomer Brahmagupta wrote some important works on both mathematics and astronomy. ... Brahmagupta established the basic mathematical rules for dealing with zero (1 + 0 = 1; 1 – 0 = 1; and 1 x 0 = 0).

checks.reason: Cited MacTutor page fetched and supports both claims verbatim: Brahmagupta gave rules for arithmetic with zero in the 7th century (Brahmasphutasiddhanta, 628 CE) including 'the sum of zero and zero is zero', and MacTutor names him 'the first person that we know who tried to extend arithmetic to negative numbers and zero'. The Babylonian 400 BC two-wedge placeholder is also stated on the same page. No distractor century is defensible (Aryabhata's 5th-century zero symbol and the disputed ~200 AD placeholders are placeholders, not arithmetic rules; the 2nd/12th/17th centuries are not argued by any source). Content is benign and reading level suits 8-10.

items.question: Which of these numbers has only one factor?
items.fact: 1 has only one factor: itself. A prime number is a whole number bigger than 1 whose only factors are 1 and itself, so 2, 3 and 5 are prime and 1 is not counted as prime. Leaving 1 out means every number can be built from primes in exactly one way.

sources.title: Wolfram MathWorld: Prime Number
sources.quote: A prime number (or prime integer, often simply called a 'prime' for short) is a positive integer p>1 that has no positive integer divisors other than 1 and p itself. … A good reason not to call 1 a prime number is that if 1 were prime, then the statement of the fundamental theorem of arithmetic would have to be modified since 'in exactly one' way would be false because any n=n·1.

checks.reason: PrimePages (t5k.org), independent of Wolfram MathWorld, defines a prime as an integer greater than one whose only positive divisors are one and itself, states explicitly that 1 is not prime, and gives the unique-factorization (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic) reason for excluding 1. Answer, distractors and fact text all check out.
checks.source_title: PrimePages (t5k.org): Why is the number one not prime?
checks.quote: An integer greater than one is called a prime number if its only positive divisors (factors) are one and itself. ... Every positive integer greater than one can be written uniquely as a product of primes.

checks.reason: Cited MathWorld page fetched and supports the definition (positive integer p>1) and the fundamental-theorem-of-arithmetic reason for excluding 1. The page notes 1 was historically called prime (Goldbach 1742, Lehmer 1909), but the modern convention is universal and the fact text says 1 'is not counted as prime', which is correct. Distractors 2, 3, 5 are all unambiguously prime. No timeliness issue; content benign; reading level suits 8-10.

items.question: On which date is Pi Day celebrated every year?
items.fact: Pi Day is 14 March because, written the American way, that is 3/14, the first digits of pi (3.14159...). Physicist Larry Shaw started it at the Exploratorium science museum in San Francisco in 1988, and it is now celebrated all over the world.

items.question: If you start at 1 and double it 10 times, what number do you reach?

items.fact: A Möbius strip is made by giving a paper band a half twist before joining its ends. The result has only one side and one edge. Two mathematicians, August Möbius and Johann Listing, each found it on their own in 1858. Listing wrote about it first, but the strip is named after Möbius.

sources.quote: The Möbius strip, also called the twisted cylinder (Henle 1994, p. 110), is a one-sided nonorientable surface obtained by cutting a closed band into a single strip, giving one of the two ends thus produced a half twist, and then reattaching the two ends ... The strip bearing his name was invented by Möbius in 1858, although it was independently discovered by Listing, who published it, while Möbius did not

sources.title: August Ferdinand Möbius - MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews
sources.quote: A Möbius strip is a two-dimensional surface with only one side.

checks.reason: Independently confirmed. The Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry on Möbius (encyclopedia.com) states Möbius 'discovered this surface around September 1858' and published it in 'Ueber die Bestimmung des Inhaltes eines Polyëders' of 1865, while 'Johann Benedict Listing discovered the same surface in July 1858 and published his discovery in 1861' — so 'Listing discovered it independently and published it first' is accurate. Cut-the-Knot confirms it is the first one-sided surface, made by twisting one end 180 degrees (a half turn) and gluing, and that Listing described it independently two months earlier; Encyclopedia of Mathematics confirms it is one-sided and was considered independently by Möbius and Listing in 1858-1865; Plus magazine confirms the boundary is a single closed curve (one edge). Answer 1 is correct; distractors fine.
checks.source_title: August Ferdinand Möbius - Complete Dictionary of Scientific Biography (Encyclopedia.com)
checks.quote: Johann Benedict Listing discovered the same surface in July 1858 and published his discovery in 1861.

checks.reason: Cited quotes verified verbatim on MathWorld and MacTutor. 'One edge' is independently confirmed by Wikipedia ('It has only a single boundary curve'). The priority claim holds: MacTutor's Möbius biography says 'by any criterion, either publication date or date of first discovery, precedence goes to Listing', and MathWorld says Listing published it while Möbius did not. Answer 1 is the universal mathematical answer; no distractor is arguable. Only weakness: the history sentence ('discovered it independently and published it first') is dense for an 8-10 reading age and slightly implies Möbius also published, so a simpler reword is supplied. Note the shape itself appears in Roman mosaics, but the fact's claim is about its mathematical discovery, which is standard.
checks.source_title: Möbius strip - Wikipedia
checks.quote: The discovery of the Möbius strip as a mathematical object is attributed independently to the German mathematicians Johann Benedict Listing and August Ferdinand Möbius in 1858.

items.question: A classic symmetrical snowflake has how many arms or sides?
items.fact: A classic snow crystal has six-fold symmetry, with six sides or six arms. That symmetry comes from the way water molecules are arranged in the ice crystal lattice, which is hexagonal.

sources.title: Snow Crystal Science - SnowCrystals.com (Kenneth Libbrecht, Caltech)
sources.quote: The six-fold symmetry you see in a snow crystal arises from the arrangement of water molecules in the ice crystal lattice.

sources.title: The Beauty and Science of Snowflakes - Smithsonian Science Education Center
sources.quote: The 'classic' snowflake is a six-sided crystal, but variations in humidity and temperature can alter its shape.

checks.reason: Independently confirmed. The UK Met Office 'Snowflakes' page states all snowflakes have six sides or points and attributes it to the molecules in ice crystals joining in a hexagonal structure; NOAA's 'How do snowflakes form?' story confirms 'symmetrical, six-sided snowflakes'; Wikipedia's Snowflake article adds that six-fold symmetry arises from the hexagonal crystalline structure of ice. Answer 6 correct; the fact's causal claim (hexagonal ice lattice) is accurate; distractors 4, 5, 8 are clean.
checks.source_title: Snowflakes - Met Office
checks.quote: All snowflakes contain six sides or points owing to the way in which they form. ... The molecules in ice crystals join to one another in a hexagonal structure

checks.reason: Both cited quotes verified verbatim (SnowCrystals.com and the Smithsonian SSEC blog). Wikipedia independently confirms the six-fold symmetry arises 'from the hexagonal crystalline structure of ice'. Real-world exceptions are twelve-branched crystals (which still have six-fold symmetry) and rare triangular crystals; none of the distractors (4, 5, 8) occur naturally, so none can be argued correct. The word 'classic' in the question correctly hedges against irregular flakes. No rot risk, no danger content, reading age fine.
checks.source_title: Snowflake - Wikipedia
checks.quote: Very occasionally twelve branched snowflakes are observed; they maintain the six-fold symmetry.

items.question: An empty elevator car weighs 1000 kg and its counterweight weighs 1500 kg. Then 300 kg of people get in. Now how much heavier is the counterweight than the car with the people inside?
items.fact: An elevator counterweight is usually set to the weight of the empty car plus 40 to 50% of the load the elevator is rated to carry. It moves the opposite way to the car, so the motor only has to lift the difference in weight. Here the car with people weighs 1000 + 300 = 1300 kg, and 1500 - 1300 = 200 kg.

sources.title: Counterweights - TK Elevator Classroom On Demand
sources.quote: The weight of an elevator cab (structural load) plus part of the passenger load (40 to 50% of its rated load) determines the weight of the counterweights. ... The weights travel up and down in the opposite direction from the elevator cab.

checks.reason: Independently confirmed. Explain That Stuff ('How do elevators work?') states the counterweight weighs the car itself plus 40-50 percent of the total weight it can carry, moves down when the car goes up and vice versa, and that the motor only has to lift the difference in weight between the two; Wikipedia's Elevator article agrees ('equal to the weight of the elevator cab plus 40-50% of the capacity'). Arithmetic verified: 1500 - (1000 + 300) = 200 kg. The premise is consistent (1500 - 1000 = 500 kg implies a 1000-1250 kg rated load, and 300 kg of passengers fits). Distractors are the natural wrong-path answers (500 = ignoring passengers, 1200 = ignoring the car, 800 = adding instead of subtracting) and none equals the answer.
checks.source_title: How do elevators and lifts work? - Explain that Stuff
checks.quote: The elevator car is balanced by a heavy counterweight that weighs roughly the same amount as the car when it's loaded half-full (in other words, the weight of the car itself plus 40–50 percent of the total weight it can carry).

checks.reason: Arithmetic is correct: 1500 - (1000 + 300) = 200. The cited TK Elevator page was fetched and does contain both quoted sentences (40 to 50% of rated load; weights travel opposite to the cab). Wikipedia independently confirms 'cab plus 40-50% of the capacity'. Two defects rescued by the fix: (1) the question says 'heavier than the car', and a literal reader (especially an autistic child) can take 'the car' as the 1000 kg car alone, which gives exactly the distractor 500 kg, so the question must say 'the car with the people inside'; (2) the TK page does not support 'the motor only has to move the difference' (the motor still moves all the mass; it only has to LIFT the net difference), so the fact is reworded to 'lift the difference in weight', which matches Wikipedia's 'reduces the amount of power needed'. No danger content; the arithmetic is suitable for ages 10-12 at difficulty 3.
checks.source_title: Elevator - Wikipedia
checks.quote: The weight of the counterweight is typically equal to the weight of the elevator cab plus 40–50% of the capacity of the elevator.

items.question: The Burj Khalifa's fastest elevators climb 10 metres every second; if each floor were 4 metres tall, how many floors would they pass each second?
items.fact: Otis's double-deck elevators in the Burj Khalifa run at up to 10 metres per second (as of 2024) and reach the observation deck on floors 124 and 125 in about 60 seconds. If each floor were 4 metres tall, 10 divided by 4 would give 2.5 floors every second.

sources.title: Otis Wins Modernization Project and 10-Year Service Contract Extension for Burj Khalifa - Otis Worldwide press release (PR Newswire, 2024)
sources.quote: Two double-deck elevators travel at speeds of up to 10 meters per second, taking passengers from the ground floor to the observation deck on the 124th and 125th floors in just 60 seconds.

checks.reason: Otis's own investor-relations release (6 March 2024, a different site from the PR Newswire copy the researcher used) states two double-deck elevators run at up to 10 m/s and reach the observation deck on the 124th and 125th floors in 60 seconds; Wikipedia's Burj Khalifa article independently confirms the world's fastest double-deck elevators at up to 10 m/s. The 4 m per floor is a stipulation in the question, and 10/4 = 2.5 is correct. Only sloppiness: no as-of date on a spec that comes from a 2024 announcement.
checks.source_title: Otis Wins Modernization Project and 10-Year Service Contract Extension for Burj Khalifa - Otis Investor Relations (6 March 2024)
checks.quote: To transport passengers to the top, two double-deck elevators travel at speeds of up to 10 meters per second, taking passengers from the ground floor to the observation deck on the 124th and 125th floors in just 60 seconds.

checks.reason: Cited PR Newswire release (fetched, dated 6 March 2024) says exactly what the researcher quoted: two double-deck elevators at up to 10 m/s, ground to floors 124/125 in 60 seconds. Wikipedia independently confirms 10 m/s and the 124th-floor deck at 452 m. Arithmetic is correct and no distractor is defensible. One weakness: real Burj Khalifa floors average ~3.65 m (452 m / 124 floors), so the 4-metre figure is a made-up simplification; the question says 'if', but the fact text asserts 'At 4 metres per floor' as though true. Fixed by making the fact conditional and adding an as-of year (a modernization project is underway).

items.question: To do 9 times 4 on your hands you hold up ten fingers and fold down the 4th finger from the left; fingers to its left are tens and fingers to its right are ones, so what answer do you get?
items.fact: With the 4th finger folded down, three fingers stand to its left (the tens) and six to its right (the ones), giving 36, which is 9 times 4. The trick works for 9 times 1 up to 9 times 10, one for each finger.

sources.title: Multiplication Tricks - UVU Math Lab, Utah Valley University
sources.quote: Hand Method: 1. Hold up ten fingers. 2. Count over from the left the number of fingers equal to the multiplier. 3. Hold that finger down. 4. The number of fingers to the left of the multiplier is the tens place of the solution. 5. The number of fingers to the right is in the ones place of the solution.

checks.reason: Math Kids and Chaos (independent of UVU) describes exactly the method: fold down the nth finger from the left, fingers to its left are tens, fingers to its right are ones, with worked examples 3x9=27 and 7x9=63; Maths Is Fun independently gives the same trick (8th finger down, count 7 and 2 = 72). Folding the 4th finger leaves 3 left and 6 right = 36, and the trick covers 9x1 through 9x10 because there are ten fingers. Fact text is accurate as written.
checks.source_title: Top tips and tricks for learning the 9 times table - Math, Kids and Chaos
checks.quote: The folded down finger will act as our divide between the tens and ones in our answer. The fingers to the left of the folded finger represent the number of tens (the tens digit), and the fingers to the right of the folded finger represent the number of ones

checks.reason: Read the cited UVU Math Lab PDF directly: the Hand Method steps match the researcher's quote word for word, and the handout's worked example (9 x 3, showing 2 fingers left and 7 right) confirms the procedure. For 9 x 4 the 4th finger folds, leaving 3 left and 6 right = 36. Distractors 27, 45, 63 are 9x3, 9x5, 9x7, none arguable. The claim that it works for 9x1 to 9x10 checks (9x10 gives 9 left, 0 right = 90). Child-appropriate; no fix needed.
checks.source_title: Multiplication Tricks - UVU Math Lab, Utah Valley University
checks.quote: The number of fingers to the left of the multiplier is the tens place of the solution.

items.question: In what year did Robert Recorde first print the equals sign, =, in a maths book?
items.fact: Robert Recorde introduced the = sign in his 1557 book The Whetstone of Witte. He chose a pair of parallel lines 'bicause noe .2. thynges, can be moare equalle' (because no two things can be more equal).

sources.title: Robert Recorde - MacTutor History of Mathematics, University of St Andrews
sources.quote: The Whetstone of Witte published in 1557 ... bicause noe 2 thynges can be moare equalle

checks.reason: Confirmed by three non-MacTutor sources: the plover.com transcription gives 1557 and the full original passage; BBC News (16 Sept 2015) gives 1557, The Whetstone of Witte and the 'noe 2 thynges can be moare equalle' quotation; MathWorld gives 1557 and the book title. Answer and fact are correct; the fixed version restores Recorde's original punctuation ('.2.' and the comma) for fidelity.
checks.source_title: Robert Recorde invents the equals sign - The Universe of Discourse (plover.com); also BBC News, 'Tenby man who invented the equals sign remembered in exhibit', 16 Sept 2015
checks.quote: The Whetstone of Witte that contains the world's first use, in 1557, of the equals sign. ... a pair of paralleles, or Gemowe lines of one lengthe, thus: =====, bicause noe .2. thynges, can be moare equalle.

checks.reason: MacTutor (cited, fetched) confirms The Whetstone of Witte was published in 1557 and carries the 'noe 2 thynges can be moare equalle' justification. Wikipedia's Equals sign article independently confirms Recorde first recorded = in that 1557 book and notes the symbol was not printed again until 1618. Earlier equality notations (Diophantus's abbreviation, the word 'aequales') were not the = symbol in print, so the question's 'first print' wording is safe. Distractors 1453, 1687, 1801 are not defensible. The Tudor spelling is hard for the reading age but the fact supplies a translation. No fix needed.
checks.source_title: Equals sign - Wikipedia
checks.quote: The Whetstone of Witte (1557) ... because no 2 things can be more equal

items.question: If you fold a sheet of A4 paper in half so its two short edges meet, what paper size is the folded sheet?
items.fact: Every sheet in the A series is the same shape: its long side is about 1.4 times its short side (the square root of 2). Because of that, halving a sheet's longer side gives two smaller sheets of exactly the same shape. A4 is 210 by 297 mm, and half of it is A5, 148 by 210 mm.

sources.title: International standard paper sizes - Markus Kuhn, University of Cambridge Computer Laboratory
sources.quote: In the ISO paper size system, the height-to-width ratio of all pages is the square root of two (1.4142 : 1). ... cut one parallel to its shorter side into two equal pieces, then the resulting page will have again the same width/height ratio. ... A4 210 × 297

checks.reason: papersizes.org (independent of the Cambridge page) gives A4 = 210 x 297 mm, A5 = 148 x 210 mm, the 1.4142 length-to-width ratio, and that each A(n) is A(n-1) cut in half parallel to its shorter sides; Wikipedia's ISO 216 article confirms A5 is half of A4 and the sqrt(2) self-similarity. Answer correct. The fact's phrase 'across its shorter side' is ambiguous about the cut direction; fixed to 'parallel to its shorter side' to match the question's 'short edges meet'.
checks.source_title: A Paper Sizes - A0, A1, A2, A3, A4, A5, A6, A7, A8, A9, A10 - papersizes.org
checks.quote: The length divided by the width is 1.4142 ... Each subsequent size A(n) is defined as A(n-1) cut in half parallel to its shorter sides. ... A4 210 x 297 mm ... A5 148 x 210 mm

checks.reason: Kuhn's Cambridge page (cited, fetched) confirms the sqrt(2) ratio, that cutting parallel to the shorter side preserves the shape, and A4 = 210 x 297 mm, A5 = 148 x 210 mm. Folding so the short edges meet halves the 297 mm side, giving 148.5 x 210 = A5; A3 is larger, A6 is a quarter sheet, A2 is larger still, so no distractor works. The fact's phrase 'cutting a sheet in half across its shorter side' is ambiguous (a cut running across the short side would halve the wrong dimension); reworded to 'halving its longer side' and simplified the square-root sentence for an 8-10 reading age.

checks.quote: cut one parallel to its shorter side into two equal pieces, then the resulting page will have again the same width/height ratio
